operationalization: For each named domesticate, score whether a living or historically documented wild population of the same species, or its accepted wild progenitor, exists. The generalization holds if wild counterparts are present for nearly all of those kinds; it fails if tameness tracks a species boundary in most of them.

candidate_datasets.name: DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: inventory of domesticated breeds of horse, cattle, dog, pig, goat and sheep

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomy of the wild equids, bovids, wolves, boar, bezoar and mouflon against which the domestic forms are compared

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts stating which of these mammals occur as wild populations

obstacles: Tame and wild are population statuses, not always species differences, and the aurochs is extinct.
Dogs in India and humans do not map cleanly onto a wild-versus-domestic species pair.
rationale: Breed inventories and mammal taxonomy already record wild relatives for the livestock named in the passage, so the listed examples can be checked without new fieldwork. The quantifier almost all, and the inclusion of humans, still require a judgment about which kinds belong in the set. That keeps the test short of the full scope even though the named mammals are well covered.

operationalization: Ask whether the folk classes Birds and Fishes are recovered as clusters by many morphological characters together, and whether a single-character dichotomous key fails to recover those same groups. The methodological ought is not itself a measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: tests whether the folk classes birds and fishes correspond to phylogenetic groups

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: multi-trait morphological matrix for birds, to see whether the class is defined by many characters rather than one

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic and morphological coverage of fishes as a candidate natural group

obstacles: The claim is a prescription about method, so agreement with phylogeny does not decide that dichotomy must be abandoned.
Fishes are not a single clade, which complicates the folk group Aristotle treats as natural.
rationale: Character matrices and a global tree can show that birds, and less cleanly fishes, are multi-trait clusters rather than one-character cuts. They cannot decide the normative claim that classification ought to follow instinctive groups. Discriminating power stays modest because several rival classifications are compatible with the same matrices.

operationalization: Within birds, test whether corresponding parts differ by continuous degree. Between birds and fishes, test whether feathers and scales are the same part or only functionally similar. A within-class gap as large as the feather-scale gap, or a developmental identity of feather and scale, would count against the stated contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: continuous plumage-related and body measurements within birds

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: scale and body-form records for the fish side of the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical classes that separate a feather from a scale when homology is being scored

obstacles: Analogy versus sameness of part is theory-laden and can be circular with the classification.
Feather and scale identity is a developmental question, not a measurement AVONET records directly.
rationale: Open bird measurements can test the more-and-less half inside one class. The cross-class claim depends on whether feather and scale are scored as the same organ, which existing trait tables do not decide by themselves. Coverage of fishes is broad for taxonomy and thin for a matched part-by-part matrix.

operationalization: Tabulate, for vertebrates and the main invertebrate groups, the respiratory organ and the circulating fluid, and score whether the fluid carries respiratory gases. The claim fails if a lungless group has no respiratory substitute, or if the bloodless fluid does not do the work attributed to blood.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gills, lungs and air-breathing across fishes

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: respiratory structures of marine invertebrates that lack vertebrate blood

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: standard terms for lung, gill and circulatory fluid so substitutes are scored consistently

obstacles: Same office is clear for gills versus lungs and much less clear for insect hemolymph, which often does not carry oxygen.
Aristotle's bloodless animals lump several phyla with different fluids.
rationale: Respiratory anatomy of fishes and marine invertebrates is already tabulated well enough to test the existence of substitutes for lungs. The functional claim that the substitute fluid has the office of blood is only partly measured, especially in tracheate arthropods. The test therefore covers the anatomical contrast more securely than the shared-function clause.

operationalization: No measurement distinguishes the body being made for the soul, or each part for a subordinate function, from the bare observation that organs do things.
obstacles: Soul is not an observable variable.
Functional fit of a part does not separate a final cause from the fact that the part is used.
rationale: The passage states a teleological principle rather than a difference that data could confirm or refute. Any working organ is compatible with the claim, and a poorly matched organ can be redescribed as serving some other function. Existing anatomical databases would only restate the functions, which is the bare fact the explanation does not go beyond.

operationalization: Histology can show that organs are made of tissues, but no observation separates tissues existing for the sake of organs from organs simply being composed of tissues that carry out functions.
obstacles: For the sake of is not distinguished from composition plus function.
Homogeneous and heterogeneous are Aristotelian part-kinds, not a modern measurement protocol.
rationale: The compositional reading is ordinary anatomy, and it is exactly the bare fact that the final-cause clause does not add a further prediction to. A dataset of tissue types would be compatible with every rival account of why organs are built from tissues. The claim as stated therefore has no discriminating empirical test.

operationalization: Locate the structures required for sensation, locomotion and nutrition in vertebrates and in cephalopods, crustaceans and insects. The claim is supported if those faculties are abolished by disabling the heart, or its anatomical substitute, and spared by disabling the brain; the reverse result refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: maps of sensory, motor and hypothalamic regions in mouse and human brains

candidate_datasets.name: InsectBrainDB
candidate_datasets.role: central-brain reconstructions for bloodless animals, to locate sensory and motor neuropils

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish anatomy of heart versus brain as a vertebrate test case

obstacles: Open atlases cover model species, not every sanguineous and bloodless group.
Nutrition can be redescribed as circulation, which makes that third faculty less decisive than sensation.
rationale: Public brain atlases already separate sensory and motor centers from the heart in vertebrates and put the corresponding centers in the central nervous system of insects. That is enough to test the mechanism in well-studied taxa and not enough to cover Aristotle's full partition of animals. The nutrition clause remains easier to reconcile with a circulatory role than the sensory clause does.

operationalization: Measure blood viscosity and temperature, a force or power variable, and a pre-registered cognitive assay across the same species, then test the two predicted gradients. No such paired public table exists.
obstacles: Intelligence and strength have several competing operationalizations.
Blood viscosity, blood temperature, performance and cognition are not published together for a comparative sample.
rationale: The predicted gradients are measurable in principle, but no open dataset holds blood thickness, blood temperature, strength and a cognitive score for the same animals. Veterinary blood values and cognition studies sit in different literatures and barely overlap. A comparative test would have to be designed and collected, not run on current files.

operationalization: Compare clotting of shed blood with the flow of yellow bile, identified with gallbladder bile, before and after removal from the body. Clotting of blood supports the first half; bile that thickens rather than thins refutes the second.
obstacles: Clotting times are scattered through clinical and veterinary papers rather than one comparative file.
Yellow bile is not a standard fluid in modern comparative datasets, so the bile half is thinly measured.
rationale: Blood coagulation outside the body is a routine measurement for humans and domestic mammals, so that half can be checked from published tables. The claim that yellow bile becomes more fluid when separated is not a variable in any public comparative database. A full test would compile a small literature and would still be thin outside a few species.

operationalization: Score presence of a stomach, as a distinct digestive sac, across animal phyla, with a separate score for animals that move from place to place. A locomotory phylum that feeds without such a sac refutes the conspicuous half; many non-locomotory exceptions are allowed by the wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: digestive anatomy across vertebrate and invertebrate accounts

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: feeding structures of marine invertebrates, including groups that lack a stomach sac

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: a fixed class for stomach so gastrovascular cavities are not counted as the same organ

obstacles: Stomach is ambiguous for cnidarians, flatworms and animals that absorb food across a gut without a sac.
The scope is all animals, while open accounts are uneven outside vertebrates and common marine groups.
rationale: Species accounts already record a stomach for vertebrates and a gut sac for many mobile invertebrates, and they record groups that lack one. Mapping those descriptions onto Aristotle's sac, as opposed to any digestive cavity, takes interpretation and does not cover every phylum at the same resolution. The locomotory qualifier is testable for the major mobile groups and not as a complete census.

operationalization: Measure blood volume or a red-cell mass proxy in the same animals when fasted and when fed, and score whether the blood's condition tracks the food. A failure of blood quantity to move with intake refutes the observable prediction; calling blood the final nutriment needs a separate developmental test.
obstacles: Fasting-versus-fed blood volume is published for humans and a few domestic species, not as a comparative dataset.
The final-nutriment identity is stronger than the quantity prediction and is not settled by volume changes.
rationale: The quantity prediction is a straightforward physiology result and has been measured in restricted settings. Those measurements are not assembled into an open multi-species dataset, and they do not show that every tissue is built from blood. The testable fragment is real and the full claim is not covered.

operationalization: For deer and roe deer, assay fibrinogen or fibrin strands and record whether shed blood forms a clot. Absence of clot and of fibrin supports the claim; a normal clot, or fibrin without a missing-fiber explanation, refutes it.
obstacles: Comparative clotting data for cervids are in veterinary papers, not a public trait table.
Roe deer is a clear species, but deer could be read as the whole family, which is only partly measured.
rationale: Fibrin content and clotting time are standard assays, and published hematology for a few deer species is enough to confront the universal never. There is no open dataset that already holds those assays across Cervidae. A small team could compile the papers; it could not download the result.

operationalization: Compare a pre-registered fear assay, plus immobility, discharge of ink or feces, and color change, between cephalopods and insects and a sample of vertebrates. The general rule fails if vertebrates show these responses as strongly as the bloodless groups do.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of inking, color change and tonic immobility in cephalopods and other invertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: ecology notes for marine invertebrates whose defensive responses are at issue

obstacles: More timorous is not a shared scale across phyla.
Color change and inking are taxon-specific acts, so they are weak evidence for a general temperament difference.
rationale: Immobility, discharge and color change are observable, and natural-history accounts document them for cephalopods and some insects. They are not coded as comparable fear measures against vertebrates, so a quantitative general rule cannot be read out of current databases. The test would be informative only after a great deal of reinterpretation.

operationalization: Rank whole-blood clotting time, and a fiber or fibrinogen measure, for bull and boar against other vertebrates. The speed claim fails if any species clots as fast as or faster than bull blood; the fiber claim fails if those two species are not extremes.
obstacles: Any other animal is a universal comparison, while published clotting times cover domestic mammals and a scattering of wildlife.
Bull and boar must be separated from the species, because sex and breed affect clotting.
rationale: Clotting time is a defined assay, and veterinary tables already compare cattle with several other domestic species. They do not approach the scope of any other animal, and fiber richness is not in an open comparative file. The existing literature can probe a restricted livestock comparison and cannot close the universal claim.

operationalization: Join dental and horn characters to the saturation or melting behavior of adipose fat. Suet is supported when horned, upper-incisorless ruminants have hard-setting fat and pigs and similar toed animals have soft fat; a ruminant with lard-like fat, or a pig with suet, refutes the pairing.

candidate_datasets.name: FoodData Central
candidate_datasets.role: fatty-acid profiles of beef tallow and pork lard as a proxy for hard-setting suet versus soft lard

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: horn presence, upper incisors and foot form for the ruminants and the pig

obstacles: Food composition tables cover livestock fats, not the fats of deer, antelope and other wild horned species.
Hard-setting is inferred from saturation, which is a proxy for the coagulation Aristotle describes.
rationale: Public food-composition data separate beef tallow from pork lard, and species accounts record the horn and tooth characters for the same domestic contrast. Wild horned mammals are outside those food tables, so the full scope is not covered. The anatomical half of the pairing is easier to finish than the fat chemistry.

operationalization: Relate a direct adiposity measure, not body mass, to litter size or another fecundity measure across blooded animals, and separately ask whether fat mass trades off with gamete production. Lower fecundity in fatter animals supports the pattern; the semen-diversion mechanism needs a physiological test of its own.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and body mass for mammals; body mass is only a proxy for the fatness the claim requires

obstacles: Life-history databases record body mass and litter size, not carcass fat.
The proposed diversion of blood from semen to suet is not measured by a fecundity correlation.
rationale: Mammal life-history tables can support a confounded proxy, mass against litter size, and cannot represent fatness. Within-species livestock studies of body condition and fertility exist as papers, not as an open comparative file. The mechanism in the explanation is a further claim those tables do not touch.

operationalization: On CT or sectioned long bones, measure marrow-cavity volume relative to bone volume in the lion and in other species scored for cortical thickness. A substantial marrow cavity in the lion refutes the specific claim; the general rule about strong solid bones needs a broader sample.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: downloadable skeletal scans, including felid long bones, for marrow-cavity volume

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT slices of mammal limbs in which a marrow cavity can be seen directly

obstacles: Open scans of lions are few, and many scans are of skulls rather than limb bones.
Strong and solid is not a pre-coded variable, so the general half needs an extra measurement protocol.
rationale: Marrow-cavity size is visible in existing CT archives, so the lion claim can be checked if suitable long-bone scans are in the repositories. Those archives do not systematically sample every animal with dense bone, and specimen coverage for Panthera leo is limited. The specific claim is much closer to a test than the general rule attached to it.

operationalization: Rank tissue temperatures of brain, blood, liver and skin in living animals, and score whether brain parenchyma contains blood vessels. The brain being warmer than another tissue, or visibly vascular, refutes the corresponding half.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: reference brain anatomy for vascular and histological structure, not for temperature

obstacles: Paired organ temperatures are published for a few mammals and are not a comparative database.
Cold to the touch in a dead or exposed brain is a different variable from temperature in life.
rationale: Both halves are measurable, and the vascular half is visible in ordinary neuroanatomy, including public brain atlases of model species. A ranking of organ temperatures across animals with brains is not an open dataset. The claim can be confronted for humans and a few laboratory or domestic mammals and not for the stated scope.

operationalization: Test the physical prediction that the brain lowers the temperature of blood in the heart region, as distinct from merely being present. A brain that is warmer than incoming blood, or that does not change cardiac temperature when its heat exchange is blocked, refutes that prediction. The appeal to nature's purpose is not an extra variable.
obstacles: Selective brain cooling, where it exists, is a different circuit from cooling the heart.
Temperature measurements are scattered across physiology papers for a few mammals.
rationale: Unlike a bare final cause, the passage predicts that brain tissue moderates heart heat, and blood and brain temperatures can decide that. The measurements exist for a small set of species and are not compiled, and they often address brain cooling rather than cardiac cooling. The purpose language adds nothing further that those temperatures would not already test.

operationalization: Score a centralized brain, as opposed to ganglia only, across vertebrates and across cephalopods, insects, crustaceans and other invertebrates. The claim fails if a vertebrate lacks a brain or if a bloodless group other than octopus has an organ that must be counted as a brain on the same criteria used for the octopus.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: vertebrate brain anatomy in a sanguineous model, standing in for the positive half

candidate_datasets.name: InsectBrainDB
candidate_datasets.role: three-dimensional insect brains, the main rival to the claim that bloodless animals lack the organ

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cephalopod coverage for the octopus exception Aristotle allows

obstacles: By analogy lets the octopus exception expand or shrink depending on how brain is defined.
Blooded and bloodless do not match vertebrates and invertebrates exactly.
rationale: Vertebrate and insect brain anatomy are both in public databases, so the presence question can be posed for the main groups. The result turns on whether an insect cerebral ganglion or a cephalopod brain counts as the organ Aristotle denies to bloodless animals. That definitional choice, which the analogy clause leaves open, keeps the test from being clean across the whole scope.

operationalization: Test whether sleep onset is produced by the brain cooling postprandial blood, using simultaneous sleep state, brain temperature and blood temperature. Sleep without that cooling, or cooling without sleep, refutes the mechanism. Showing only that sleep is a brain state tests a weaker proxy.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: public sleep recordings showing sleep as a change in brain state, without the blood-cooling mechanism

obstacles: Open sleep archives do not pair brain and blood temperatures with a meal.
The analogue of the brain in brainless animals is not identified in those archives.
rationale: Public sleep datasets can show that sleep is organized in the brain, which bears on the cause half only as a proxy. They do not contain the chilling of blood after food that the mechanism requires. Temperature-and-sleep experiments exist as papers for a few mammals and would have to be compiled before the stated mechanism could be accepted or rejected.

operationalization: Compute brain mass divided by body mass for humans and the other vertebrates in the compilations, and compare men with women where sex is recorded. Any species with a higher ratio refutes the cross-animal claim; a female mean as high as the male mean refutes the sex claim. Encephalization residuals can be reported beside the ratio but are not the stated criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal brain-size allometry
candidate_datasets.role: brain and body mass for more than a thousand mammal species, with sex when the source reported it

candidate_datasets.name: Vertebrate brain and body mass
candidate_datasets.role: brain and body mass for mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fishes, the scope needed for a largest-ratio claim

obstacles: Sex is missing for many non-human rows, so the male-female contrast is essentially a human comparison.
Some small species have uncertain body masses, which moves the ratio more than absolute brain size.
rationale: Two open compilations already contain the two masses the proportion requires, across thousands of species and all major vertebrate classes. A ratio can be computed directly, and a single well-measured smaller animal with a higher ratio decides the superlative. The sex comparison is narrower because most rows are not sexed, but human male and female values are inside the same literature the mammal file draws on.

operationalization: Record the age at which the anterior fontanelle, the bregmatic gap, closes in humans and in other blooded animals that have a neonatal skull. Closure as late as or later than the human age in another species refutes the only-man clause; an earlier-closing human suture refutes the last-to-solidify clause.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal and juvenile skulls in which an open fontanelle can be scored

obstacles: Human closure ages are in clinical series, while other mammals are represented by sparse juvenile scans.
Fontanelles occur in many newborn mammals, so the only-man claim needs a timing comparison, not presence alone.
rationale: The human timetable is well measured, and open skeletal archives include some juvenile skulls that show whether a fontanelle is still open. They do not provide closure ages across blooded animals. A restricted comparison is possible; the uniqueness claim is not resolved by the scans now online.

operationalization: Count cranial sutures, or score suture complexity if number is read that way, in humans and other mammals, with a male-female contrast. More sutures in a non-human, or no sex difference, refutes the corresponding clause. The ventilation explanation is a separate claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: mammal and human skull meshes on which suture number or complexity can be counted

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: one male and one female human head as a minimal sex comparison, not a sample

obstacles: Suture number and suture complexity are competing readings of more sutures.
The human sex comparison needs a series, and the Visible Human pair is only two individuals.
rationale: Skull repositories make a count possible for a modest set of species, and human osteology has studied sex differences in sutures. Neither source is a finished table of suture counts across animals and sexes. The ventilation rationale is not tested by the count at all.

operationalization: Score whether the mineralized skeleton of crustaceans and of shelled molluscs lies outside the soft tissues. The heat-retention clause needs a separate measurement of heat loss with and without the shell, which position alone does not provide.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: body-form and skeleton notes for crustaceans and shelled molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: taxon boundaries for crustaceans and testaceans so the scope can be fixed

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans showing external cuticle or shell versus internal soft tissue

obstacles: Keeping in natural heat is not separated from protection by the mere position of the shell.
Some crustaceans are weakly calcified, so outside and hard need explicit thresholds.
rationale: External shells and cuticles are standard fields of marine species databases and are visible in scans, so the positional claim is open to a direct check. The further claim that the shell retains a small store of heat is not in those sources. Position confirms the anatomy and leaves the thermal function untested.

operationalization: Score an internal shell, cuttlebone or gladius, as present or absent in cuttlefishes, squids and octopuses. Presence in octopus, or absence in cuttlefish or squid, refutes the corresponding clause. The short body-sac explanation is not required for that anatomical test.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cephalopod morphology, including internal shell, cuttlebone and pen

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: separates Sepiidae, decapod squids and Octopoda so the three groups are not mixed

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans of cuttlebone, gladius and shell-less octopus bodies

obstacles: A few octopuses and the vampire squid complicate a blanket absence.
Calamary in Aristotle is the squid group, not one modern species.
rationale: The three shell conditions are group-level characters already recorded for cephalopods and visible in specimens. The groups Aristotle names map onto cuttlefishes, squids and octopuses without a serious ambiguity. Exceptions inside those groups are themselves in the same databases, so the universal wording can be confirmed or narrowed with data already public.

operationalization: Search skeletal scans for bones in the abdominal wall, counting gastralia, a plastron and abdominal ribs as bones of that wall. Any such element refutes the universal absence. The expansion and pregnancy rationales are not tested by presence alone.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of crocodilians and turtles, where gastralia and the plastron are abdominal bone

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: broader skeletal sample for checking whether the belly wall is free of bone

obstacles: Whether a turtle plastron counts as the belly wall is an anatomical judgment, though gastralia are a clearer case.
The functional clauses about meals and fetuses are not in the skeletal archives.
rationale: A universal absence is refuted by existing scans that show abdominal bones in crocodilians and a bony ventral shell in turtles. Those specimens are already public, and scoring them is ordinary comparative anatomy. The reasons Aristotle gives for the absence are not resolved by the same images, but the absence claim itself is.

operationalization: Compare bone mineral density or indentation hardness between sexes within species, and between carnivores and herbivores after accounting for size and phylogeny. Higher or equal female hardness, or no diet difference, refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet categories that define the carnivore and herbivore sides of the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skeletal scans that could support hardness only where density is calibrated, which most scans are not

obstacles: Most open CT scans are not calibrated to bone mineral density.
Diet and phylogeny are confounded, and sexed hardness series are scattered in papers.
rationale: Diet classes are already tabulated, so the groups in the comparison can be defined. The hardness measurements themselves are not an open cross-species, sex-specific dataset, and uncalibrated scans do not substitute for them. Published values could support a partial livestock or zoo comparison after months of harmonization.

operationalization: Strike dry and fresh lion bone with a standard striker and record whether sparks are produced, with a stone and ordinary mammal bone as controls. Sparks support the claim; none refute it. Hardness alone is not the stated result.
obstacles: No public series records percussion sparks from lion bone.
Museum specimens could be tested, but that would be new observation rather than analysis of existing data.
rationale: The observation is simple and decisive, and it is not sitting in a materials database or a skeletal archive. Scans can show density and cannot show sparks. Resolving the claim requires a new trial on specimens, not a reanalysis of current files.

operationalization: Inspect dolphin skeletons for bone with marrow spaces versus the calcified spines of a teleost. Spines in place of limb and vertebral bone would refute the claim; a bony skeleton supports it. Viviparity is used only to identify the animal, not as a separate result.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: dolphin and bony-fish skeletons for the bone-versus-spine contrast

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT slices that show cetacean bone structure rather than fish spines

obstacles: Delphinidae is a family, while Aristotle's dolphin is the Mediterranean animal; the skeletal contrast does not depend on the species.
rationale: Dolphin skeletons are standard museum objects and are present in open 3D repositories, as are teleost skeletons for the contrast. The distinction between bone and fish spine is unambiguous on those specimens. A small team can score it directly from existing scans.

operationalization: Score cartilage versus bone in the axial skeleton of sharks and rays, and compare them with undulatory bony fishes such as eels. Cartilage supports the anatomical clause; bone in a selachian refutes it. If bony fishes undulate with a brittle skeleton, the requirement that undulation needs cartilage is refuted even when the cartilage is real.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: fish skeletal phenotypes, including cartilaginous versus bony skeleton

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: identifies sharks, rays and undulatory bony fishes and their body form

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans of chondrichthyan and teleost skeletons for the tissue contrast

obstacles: Aristotle's selachians are close to living chondrichthyans but the boundary should be checked species by species.
Swimming mode is coarser in the databases than a kinematic series.
rationale: Cartilage as the skeletal tissue of sharks and rays is a standard character in fish phenotype databases and in scans. Bony fishes that also swim by undulation are in the same sources, so the functional requirement can be separated from the phylogenetic fact. Both halves of the statement can be scored with data already public.

operationalization: Treat regrowth of an amputated or cast skeletal element, not merely fracture bridging, as the variable. Regrowth of antler bone or of a salamander limb refutes the universal denial. The claim that cartilage and bone differ only by degree is a separate, looser comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: documents annual antler regeneration in deer and limb regeneration in some salamanders

obstacles: Antler casting is scheduled loss, not a cut, so a strict reading may set it aside.
Regeneration is described in species accounts and reviews, not as a presence-absence matrix for every bony animal.
rationale: Open species accounts already describe bone that is replaced each year in deer and limbs that regrow in salamanders, which is enough to put pressure on a universal negative. A strict amputated-element definition, and the lack of a complete regeneration table, keep the result short of a finished survey. The degree-difference clause is not decided by those counterexamples.

operationalization: Separate two tests: whether brain parenchyma itself is pain-sensitive, and whether sensation survives destruction or stimulation of the brain but not of the heart region. Insensate tissue can be true while the denial that the brain causes sensation is false.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: localization of sensory pathways in the brain rather than the heart

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: vertebrate neural anatomy linking sense organs to the brain

obstacles: Insensate parenchyma and not the cause of sensation are different claims and can come apart.
The atlases are model species, not a survey of all animals with brains.
rationale: Public neuroanatomical atlases place the sensory pathways in the brain, which directly addresses the denial that the brain is the cause of sensation. They do not by themselves measure whether brain tissue feels pain, and they cover laboratory vertebrates rather than every brain-bearing animal. The heart-as-center alternative is the rival those atlases are already built to discriminate.

operationalization: Score an external ear pinna, as opposed to an auditory opening or tympanum, as present or absent in birds and in scaly oviparous quadrupeds. A pinna in either group refutes the absence claim. The material explanation from feathers and scales is not part of that score.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: external-ear descriptions for birds and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: head scans of birds, lizards, turtles and crocodilians showing the auditory opening

obstacles: Crocodile ear flaps and lizard tympana must be coded separately from a mammalian pinna.
The feather-and-scale explanation of why ears are absent is not tested by presence data.
rationale: Absence of an external pinna is a gross character already described for birds and reptiles and visible on head scans. The living groups are few enough at ordinal level that a team can score them from open accounts and images. Ambiguous flaps should be coded explicitly, and once they are, the absence claim is decidable.

operationalization: Score external pinnae in phocid seals, otariid seals and other viviparous quadrupeds. No pinna in the Mediterranean monk seal supports the local claim; a pinna in another viviparous quadruped that is not being counted as eared, or in phocids, refutes uniqueness.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: pinna presence in earless seals, eared seals and other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: separates Phocidae from Otariidae so the seal of the passage can be mapped

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: seal skulls; the external ear itself is soft tissue and often absent from the scan

obstacles: English seal covers both earless and eared seals, which differ in pinnae.
Alone among viviparous quadrupeds needs a mammal-wide pinna character that is not a single downloaded column.
rationale: Species accounts distinguish earless seals from sea lions, so the Mediterranean animal Aristotle means can be checked, and so can the obvious rival groups. Uniqueness among all viviparous quadrupeds is a larger compilation than those accounts already provide as a table. Soft-tissue pinnae are also poorly represented in skeletal scans.

operationalization: Code upper eyelid, lower eyelid and nictitating membrane, and which one closes the eye, for mammals, reptiles and birds. Use of the upper lid by a heavy bird or a lizard, or absence of a nictitating membrane in birds, refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: eyelid and nictitating-membrane descriptions for mammals, reptiles and birds

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: head anatomy of reptiles and birds where eyelids are sometimes visible

obstacles: Eyelid use is behavioral and is not a column in trait databases; it has to be taken from descriptions.
Heavy-bodied birds are not a formal taxon.
rationale: The three eyelid structures are standard anatomical facts and are described across the groups named. They are not a downloadable character matrix, so a team would compile accounts for orders rather than query one file. The behaviors, which lid blinks, are less completely recorded than the presence of a nictitating membrane in birds.

operationalization: Compare visual acuity, in cycles per degree or a equivalent, between taloned birds that hunt from above and ground-living fowl. Equal or higher acuity in the fowl refutes the contrast. Foraging height can be checked separately and does not substitute for acuity.

candidate_datasets.name: Visual acuity compilation
candidate_datasets.role: published acuity measurements across animals, including raptors and some other birds

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging stratum, to separate aerial hunters from ground birds, not to measure acuity

obstacles: Acuity has been measured for few raptors and fewer galliforms.
Sharp-sighted can mean resolution, sensitivity or detection distance, which do not rank species the same way.
rationale: A published acuity compilation and a complete foraging-stratum table together define the comparison, but the acuity sample is a subset of both groups. Foraging from aloft is well coded and is only the ecological premise, not the visual result. The contrast can be tested for the species that have been measured and not for raptors and fowl as wholes.

operationalization: Score eyelids, including a nictitating membrane, as present or absent in fishes, insects and crustaceans, and score eye mobility in the latter two. A true eyelid in any of the three refutes the absence claim if the coding rules are fixed in advance.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fish morphology, including sharks in which a nictitating membrane has to be distinguished from an eyelid

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: eye covering and eye mobility in insects and crustaceans

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: structured fish phenotypes for cranial and ocular characters

obstacles: Shark nictitating membranes are the borderline case and are easy to mis-code as eyelids or as nothing.
Insect and crustacean eye mobility is described qualitatively, not as a dataset of movement ranges.
rationale: Absence of eyelids is widely described for these groups, with a known complication in sharks that have a nictitating membrane. Fish databases and species accounts cover that complication unevenly, and they do not tabulate eye movement. The absence claim is testable for a large sample; the compensation-by-movable-eyes clause is only sparsely measured.

operationalization: Score eyelashes on the eyelids of hairy mammals, birds, scaly reptiles and the ostrich. Lashes in a bird other than the ostrich, or in a scaly reptile, or their absence in a hairy mammal, refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: hair, feather and scale descriptions, including the ostrich exception where the account mentions it

obstacles: Eyelashes are rarely a structured trait; they have to be taken from prose and photographs.
Hairy mammals are too numerous for the open accounts to have been checked one by one.
rationale: The characters are externally visible and are mentioned for the ostrich and for many familiar mammals, birds and reptiles. There is no trait column for eyelashes, so coverage is a subset of species accounts rather than a census. The ostrich exception is specifically checkable; the universals over all hairy and all scaly animals are not fully covered.

operationalization: Score upper and lower eyelashes in humans and in other hairy quadrupeds. A non-human species with a developed lower eyelash refutes uniqueness; scattered hairs under the lower lid should be coded as the weaker state Aristotle already allows.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: external descriptions of mammalian eyelids and lashes for a subset of species

obstacles: Lower lashes are seldom recorded as a character, so absence in a species account is not positive evidence.
Developed lash versus a few hairs is a judgment call at the boundary the text itself notes.
rationale: The contrast is anatomically clear and can be checked from specimens and descriptions for familiar mammals. Those descriptions are not a complete public matrix of upper versus lower lashes. Uniqueness over all hairy quadrupeds therefore remains a partial compilation rather than a dataset query.

operationalization: Code the trunk as a narial structure and score the acts of bringing food and water to the mouth and of grasping or pulling vegetation. Failure of those acts, or a trunk that is not the nostril, would refute the claim. Both living elephant species are the scope.

candidate_datasets.name: ElephantVoices Ethogram
candidate_datasets.role: catalogued trunk behaviors, including feeding, drinking and grasping

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical identification of the trunk as the elongated nostrils

obstacles: The ethogram is richer for African elephants than for a balanced sample of both species.
Tearing up trees is rarer than feeding and may be sparsely coded.
rationale: A public ethogram already itemizes trunk use in feeding and manipulation, and anatomical accounts identify the trunk with the nostrils. The behaviors named are ordinary and repeatedly recorded, not anecdotes that would require a new field study. The two living species are a closed, well-observed scope.

operationalization: Score whether elephants crossing water raise the trunk above the surface and inhale through it. Observations of submerged trunks with breathing, or of no such behavior when swimming, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: ElephantVoices Ethogram
candidate_datasets.role: trunk and respiration behaviors, including use of the trunk at the water surface

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: natural-history accounts of elephants swimming and breathing through the trunk

obstacles: Quantitative rates of the behavior are thinner than the qualitative fact that it occurs.
The diver's-instrument comparison is an analogy, not a second variable.
rationale: Breathing through the raised trunk while wading or swimming is a specific, repeatedly described behavior in elephant ethograms and species accounts. It does not require new observation to establish whether it occurs. How often it occurs, and whether every crossing is handled that way, is less completely quantified.

operationalization: Rank birds by tongue width and by a mimicry or phonetic-imitation score, and compare tongue mobility in mammals. A narrow-tongued bird that imitates speech as well as broad-tongued parrots, or a highly articulating mammal with a bound tongue, weakens the association. The syrinx has to be measured or the test confounds tongue with voice organ.

candidate_datasets.name: Xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: recordings of vocal mimicry, which do not measure tongue width

obstacles: Tongue breadth is not in the bird trait matrices; it is scattered in anatomical papers.
Pronouncing letters is a human-listener category, and the syrinx, not the tongue, produces the sound.
rationale: Recordings can rank vocal imitation, but the anatomical variable the claim treats as the cause is not in those archives or in the main bird morphometric datasets. Mammal tongue mobility is likewise uncompiled. Any correlation that ignored the syrinx would not discriminate the tongue explanation from a rival vocal-organ explanation.

operationalization: Score whether each bird group produces communicative sounds and whether those sounds are produced by the tongue, plus whether any species shows tutoring. Acoustic contact without tongue involvement supports communication and refutes the tongue clause; tutoring in even one species supports the instruction clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: recordings that document vocal communication and, for some species, learned song

obstacles: The syrinx, not the tongue, is the sound source in most birds.
Instruction is stronger than shared song learning and is rarely observed directly.
rationale: A large recording archive shows that birds signal acoustically and that some songs are learned. It does not show that the tongue is the instrument, so the organ claim is confounded. Cultural transmission is documented for a subset of species in the literature behind those recordings, which tests a weak reading of instruction and not a general teaching survey.

operationalization: Score tongue length and forking in snakes and lizards against other terrestrial reptiles, and score whether the tongue delivers chemicals to the vomeronasal organ. A short unforked tongue in snakes, or forked tongues that do not sample chemicals, would refute the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic coverage of snakes and lizards; tongue shape is in descriptions rather than a trait column

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: tongue form and chemosensory use in snakes and lizards

obstacles: Many lizards have a notched tongue rather than a deep fork, so the character needs a threshold.
Suited to taste mixes contact chemoreception with smell, which modern assays separate.
rationale: Forked, protrusible tongues are described for snakes and for many lizards in open herpetological accounts, so the morphological contrast with other reptiles can be compiled. The databases do not code tongue shape as a field, and the sensory function rests on experimental papers rather than a trait file. Shape is closer to a decision than the tasting clause.

operationalization: On crocodile specimens and kinematic descriptions, score whether the tongue is fixed to the floor of the mouth and whether jaw opening includes rotation of the skull as well as depression of the lower jaw. A free tongue, or opening with an immobile skull and a mobile lower jaw only, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: alligator and crocodile head scans showing the tongue's attachment and the jaw joint

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of crocodilian tongue and jaw mechanics

obstacles: Upper jaw moves can mean skull rotation at the neck rather than a kinetic upper jaw, and the coding must say which.
Soft tongue tissue is clearer in dissections than in dry skull scans.
rationale: Crocodylidae is a small, intensively described group, and public scans plus species accounts cover tongue attachment and the contribution of skull lifting to gape. The classic ambiguity is what counts as movement of the upper jaw, and that can be fixed before looking at the specimens. Once it is fixed, existing anatomy decides the claim.

operationalization: Identify Mediterranean muricid snails with Aristotle's purpurae and score whether the radula drills other shells. Drill holes attributable to muricids support the claim; feeding without boring, or boring by a different organ, would refute the stated means.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet and feeding mode of muricid gastropods

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: drill-hole predation traces linked to boring snails

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: places purpurae in Muricidae so the taxon is not left at the ancient name

obstacles: Several muricid genera bore, so the ancient name does not pick out one species.
The fossil drill-hole record is a proxy for the living behavior Aristotle describes.
rationale: Radular drilling by purple snails is a standard, documented feeding mode in marine species databases and in the trace-fossil record of drill holes. The ancient group maps to muricids rather than to a single species, and that family-level mapping is enough for the behavior claimed. Existing records can confirm boring or show that a given species does not do it.

operationalization: Code saw-like interlocking teeth and tusks, meaning enlarged projecting canines or incisors, across mammals. One species with both refutes the exclusion. The remark that nature makes nothing in vain is not a separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulas and tusk descriptions for carnivores, pigs, walrus, hippo and chevrotains

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skulls on which carnassials and tusks can be scored together

obstacles: Tusk and saw-tooth need explicit definitions or pigs' canines and carnassials will be miscounted.
Dental formulas omit tooth shape, so prose and specimens have to be combined.
rationale: The exclusion is a presence-absence pattern over a manageable set of tusked and carnassial mammals, and both open accounts and skull scans cover those species. Shape is not a field in dental formulas, so the saw-like criterion has to be applied by hand. That is a compilation of weeks, not a missing observation, and it still leaves borderline canines to be coded.

operationalization: Weapon size can be measured, but ability to use the weapon is inferred from the use itself, so no outcome distinguishes the allotment claim from the observation that animals use the structures they have.
obstacles: Can use is not independent of observed use.
More marked degree and most perfect state can be adjusted after the fact to fit any size difference.
rationale: The sentence is a final-cause rule about allotment. Any animal that fights with a horn or spur confirms it, and an animal that rarely fights can be placed in the less developed grade without a prior criterion. Correlations of weapon size with combat do not separate that rule from the bare fact that the structures are used.

operationalization: For horns, tusks and spurs, score male-only presence versus female presence, and relative size where both sexes have the weapon. Hinds with antlers equal to stags, or hens with spurs as large as cocks, refute the stated examples; a species with the larger weapon in females refutes the general tendency.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: sex differences in antlers, horns, tusks and galliform spurs

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: sexed bird measurements; spurs are not a trait in the file and diet or body size cannot replace them

obstacles: Female antlers in reindeer and occasional spurs in hens are real boundary cases the quantifier some species must accommodate.
Weapon size is not a column in the life-history tables, so most of the work is compilation.
rationale: The named cases, deer antlers and fowl spurs, are described by sex in open species accounts and can be checked directly. A general survey of every horn, tusk and spur is not a downloaded matrix, and female weapons in caribou show why the quantifier has to be respected. The tendency is testable for the familiar taxa and incomplete for the full set of weapons.

operationalization: Code oral teeth as serrated or not across fishes, with Sparisoma cretense and close parrotfishes as the candidate Scarus. Another non-serrated dentition refutes the single exception; serrated teeth in that parrotfish refute the exception itself.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species coverage and morphological notes, including dentition when the account states it

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: structured dentition phenotypes for a subset of teleosts

obstacles: Tooth shape is not a filled field for all fishes, and beak-like parrotfish teeth are a coding boundary.
Aristotle's Scarus is usually Sparisoma cretense, but the ancient name may have been wider.
rationale: Fish databases and phenotype annotations contain dentition for many species and not as a complete serrated-versus-other column. Parrotfish jaws are well described, so the named exception can be checked, while all fishes cannot. The universal is only partly covered by data that already exist.

operationalization: Define crooked-clawed birds as raptors with talons, measure beak curvature or the ratio of beak depth to length, and read plant-food percentage from diet compilations. A straight beak, or a substantial plant fraction, in that group refutes the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: beak length, width and depth for all birds, from which a hooked beak can be operationalized

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet proportions, including plant matter, for raptors and other birds

obstacles: Hooked is a threshold on continuous beak measurements, and owls versus hawks versus falcons must be included or excluded explicitly.
Diet percentages come from mixed methods and can miss rare plant intake.
rationale: Global beak measurements and species-level diet proportions already cover every bird, including the taloned predators. A pre-registered beak-shape threshold and a plant-diet cutoff turn both clauses into ordinary comparisons. The group boundary needs to be fixed first, and once it is, the existing tables can confirm or refute the invariable association.

operationalization: Define a true horn before scoring, then ask whether that structure occurs in any egg-laying animal and whether oviparous head weapons are used in fights. Beetle horns or chameleon casques refute the claim only if the definition counts them; if true horn means the bovid organ, the restriction is nearly definitional.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: horns of ruminants contrasted with head weapons of beetles, chameleons and other egg-layers

obstacles: True versus metaphorical horn is the whole dispute, so the result follows the definition.
Used in fighting is behavioral and unevenly recorded outside mammals.
rationale: Species accounts describe mammalian horns and the head weapons of beetles and reptiles, so the structures can be listed. They do not supply a neutral definition of true horn that would let the restriction to viviparous animals be tested rather than stipulated. Fighting use is documented for some egg-laying animals and is not a complete dataset.

operationalization: For every living family that bears a head weapon called a horn or antler, score whether the weapon is solid bone and whether it is shed. Solid or deciduous weapons outside deer refute the corresponding only; hollow permanent antlers in deer would refute the deer side.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: antler bone and shedding in deer, horn sheaths in bovids, pronghorn shedding, and rhino and giraffe weapons

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: enumerates the horn-bearing families so the only-claims have a closed list

obstacles: Pronghorn sheaths and giraffe ossicones force a prior decision about what counts as a horn.
Antlers are bone and bovid horns are a keratin sheath over a core, which is the solidity contrast to be coded.
rationale: The living families with horns or antlers are few, and open accounts already say whether the structure is solid bone and whether it is cast. Pronghorns, bovids, rhinoceroses and giraffes are the decisive contrasts and are described at family level. A team can tabulate that closed set from existing references and decide both uniqueness claims.

operationalization: For every horned mammal, score upper incisors or canines in the front of the jaw. Any horned species with those teeth refutes the exclusion. The material-transfer explanation, teeth sacrificed to make horns, is not tested by the correlation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulas of bovids, deer, pronghorn, rhinoceroses and giraffes

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: closed list of living horned species so the universal can be bounded

obstacles: Rhinoceros horns and giraffe ossicones may or may not be included; the decision changes which dentitions are in scope.
Loss of tooth material into horn is a developmental claim the presence-absence table does not test.
rationale: Dental formulas for the horn-bearing mammal families are standard content of open species accounts, and the species list is finite. A single horned species with upper front teeth decides the universal negative. The causal story that horn material is tooth material diverted is a further claim and is not resolved by those formulas.

operationalization: Score lungs and a cervical region between head and pectoral girdle across vertebrates, with fishes as the stated case. A lungless animal with a neck, or a lunged animal with none, refutes the biconditional if neck is defined in advance.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gills, lungs and body form of fishes, including lungfish

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: skeletal characters of the fish pectoral region and occiput

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: definitions of lung and neck used to keep the two variables distinct

obstacles: A fish neck is anatomically disputed, so the absence can be made true by definition.
Lungfish have lungs and a poorly marked neck, which is the sensitive case.
rationale: Lung presence in fishes, including lungfish, is recorded in fish databases. Whether fishes lack a neck depends on a landmark definition that those databases do not apply uniformly. The association can be examined for tetrapods and fishes once that definition is fixed, and it is not a clean download.

operationalization: Score an epiglottis, a flap covering the laryngeal opening, across hairy mammals, birds and scaly reptiles. An epiglottis in a bird or reptile, or its absence in a hairy lunged mammal, refutes the restriction.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: laryngeal anatomy in mammal, bird and reptile accounts where it is described

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: the anatomical class epiglottis, so a laryngeal fold is not counted differently in each clade

obstacles: Epiglottis presence is not a filled trait column and must be compiled from anatomical descriptions.
Some reptile and bird laryngeal structures are easy to force into or out of the category.
rationale: The structure is well defined and is described for the major land-vertebrate classes in comparative anatomy. Those descriptions are not a single open matrix, so the universal only is a compilation across orders. Discriminating power is high once the flap is coded consistently, and the data-collection step is the limit.

operationalization: Score heart, lung, liver, spleen and kidney, or agreed homologues, in vertebrates and in cephalopods, crustaceans, molluscs and insects. A heart or digestive gland in a bloodless animal refutes the claim if homologues count; if only vertebrate organs count, the claim is nearly true by the definition of viscera.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: internal anatomy of cephalopods, crustaceans and other bloodless marine animals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: presence of hearts and digestive glands in invertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: the vertebrate viscera used as the blooded side of the contrast

obstacles: Whether a cephalopod systemic heart or an insect dorsal vessel counts as a heart decides the result.
Bloodless does not line up perfectly with invertebrates.
rationale: Internal organs of both vertebrates and the main invertebrate groups are described in open databases. The claim's force depends on refusing those invertebrate organs the name viscera, which is a homology decision rather than a missing observation. Under a strict reading the test is weak; under a homologue reading it is straightforward and unfavorable to a total absence.

operationalization: In staged embryos of blooded animals, record the first visible organ and whether blood is present in the heart at that stage. Another organ appearing before the heart, or a heart that is bloodless when first formed, refutes the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish developmental stages for the timing of heart formation and circulation

obstacles: Open staging databases cover zebrafish and a few other models, not all blooded animals.
First formed depends on the imaging method and on when a heart rudiment counts as a heart.
rationale: Vertebrate model embryos, especially zebrafish, have public stage tables that order the heart relative to other organs and show when blood cells circulate. That tests the claim in those species. It does not extend, without new comparative embryology, to every sanguineous animal Aristotle includes.

operationalization: Test whether pain, pleasure and sensation are abolished by inactivation of the heart but not of the head, using lesion, stimulation and pathway data. The opposite pattern refutes the heart as the primary seat.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Map
candidate_datasets.role: sensory and affective pathways mapped in the brain

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: human brain recordings during sensory and affective tasks

obstacles: The archives are human and model-mammal resources, not a survey of all blooded animals.
Pleasure and pain are inferred from behavior and neural markers, not observed as motions ending in the heart.
rationale: Existing brain maps and task recordings localize sensation in the head and can be set against the heart-centered alternative directly. They do not include a comparable experimental inactivation of the heart as a sensory center across taxa, because that experiment is not how the data were collected. The primary-seat claim is decidable for the studied vertebrates and not for every sanguineous animal.

operationalization: Measure the heart's midline offset in humans and in other blooded animals from dissections or imaging. A leftward apex in a non-human, or a midline human heart, refutes the corresponding uniqueness or human clause. The cold-side explanation is not part of the position test.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: human thoracic anatomy for the leftward position in one male and one female

obstacles: Veterinary imaging of heart position is published as papers, not as one comparative file.
The Visible Human sample cannot speak for other species or for humans in general.
rationale: Heart position is a routine anatomical fact, and human imaging shows the leftward tilt, but open archives do not line up the same measurement across mammals, birds and other blooded animals. A unique-to-humans claim needs that comparative series. It can be begun from textbooks and papers and cannot be finished from a single public dataset.

operationalization: Score an os cordis, a bone or cartilage in the heart skeleton, as present or absent in the horse, cattle and other mammals. Presence outside the horse and ox refutes the restriction; absence in both refutes the positive claim.
obstacles: Cardiac bones are reported in veterinary pathology papers for cattle, sheep, deer and otters, not in a trait database.
A certain kind of ox is vague, and horse records are inconsistent.
rationale: The structure is unambiguous when a heart is dissected, and published reports already name several species. Those reports are not an open survey of mammalian hearts, so the only-clause cannot be closed without compilation, and even then unsurveyed species remain. The data exist as a scattered literature rather than a dataset that contains the variable.

operationalization: Count chambers only after stating whether Aristotle's cavity is an atrium, a ventricle or a recess, then regress that count on body size. Modern four-chamber hearts in both large and small mammals refute a three-versus-two size rule under the straightforward mapping, but a different mapping can be made to fit.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: chamber anatomy of a small vertebrate heart

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: heart chamber counts in mammal, bird, reptile and fish accounts

obstacles: Aristotle's three cavities do not match the four modern chambers, so the count is unstable.
Large and small are not tied to a size cutoff.
rationale: Chamber number is basic vertebrate anatomy and is available for every class. It does not decide the claim until cavity is translated, and more than one translation is live. Under the usual modern count the size rule fails; under a charitable recount it can be preserved. That ambiguity is the main limit on discriminating power.

operationalization: Residual heart mass, after body size, is compared with a pre-registered boldness or flight-initiation measure for the hare, deer, mouse, hyena, ass, leopard, marten and a broader sample. Timid animals with small residual hearts, or bold animals with large ones, refute the direction.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: body mass for the named mammals; it does not contain heart mass or a timidity score

obstacles: Heart mass and boldness are published separately and for different species sets.
Large heart is confounded with body size unless residuals are used, and timidity is not a standard trait.
rationale: Both variables exist somewhere in the literature for some of the named species, and neither is in a joint open table. Body-size databases fix the confound only if heart weights are compiled first. The comparison is possible as a partial literature synthesis and is not a clean test with current files.

operationalization: Use fate maps to ask whether solid organs and the body wall differentiate from blood, as opposed to blood merely supplying them. A tissue lineage that does not pass through blood refutes the material claim for that tissue. Vessel layout alone does not decide it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish developmental anatomy and cell-lineage resources for whether organs arise from blood

obstacles: Lineage data are from model species, not all blooded animals.
Supply of nutrients by blood is a weaker reading that the fate maps were not designed to separate from Aristotle's stronger material claim.
rationale: Public developmental atlases of vertebrate models record germ-layer origins and can show that organs are not formed out of blood. That is a real test of the strong reading in those species. It is not a survey of every sanguineous animal, and a weak reading on which blood only nourishes the body would not be touched by lineage.

operationalization: Score gills and lungs across fishes, treating a lung in any fish as a refutation of never, and separately ask whether gill ventilation is required for cooling rather than only for gas exchange. The anatomical score and the cooling score can come apart.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: gills, lungs and air-breathing in fishes, including lungfish

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: respiratory phenotypes that separate gills from lungs

obstacles: Cooling by water is a physiological role that fish databases do not measure.
Lungfish and other air-breathers break a universal about fishes only if they are inside Aristotle's fishes.
rationale: Gill and lung presence is tabulated well enough to test the anatomical universal directly, including the lungfish counterexamples. The claim that the water is a cooling agent, rather than the medium of gas exchange, is not a field in those databases. Anatomy is resolvable with current files; the thermal function is not.

operationalization: Compare lung volume, blood content and the change in volume when inflated between mammals and the egg-laying groups, birds and reptiles. A small blood-rich mammal lung, or a large blood-filled bird lung, refutes the contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: soft-tissue or contrast scans of lungs where they exist; most specimens are skeletons

obstacles: Lung volume and blood content are in anatomical papers, not a comparative file.
Spongy and capable of great expansion need a shared inflation protocol that older descriptions do not use.
rationale: The contrast is anatomically specific and has been described for mammals, birds and reptiles. Open scan archives are dominated by bone and rarely quantify pulmonary blood or inflation. A partial comparison can be compiled from the literature; it is not a standard analysis of an existing table.

operationalization: At the level of vertebrate classes, score presence of heart, liver, lung, spleen and kidney. Absence of heart or liver in any blooded class refutes the positive claim; presence of kidney, lung or spleen in every class refutes the claim that heart and liver alone are invariable.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: class-level presence of heart, liver, lung, spleen and kidney

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: a fish reference for which of those viscera are present in a blooded animal that lacks lungs

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: confirms lung absence across most fishes while the other viscera remain in play

obstacles: Spleen tissue in jawless fishes is histologically debatable.
Class-level presence does not certify every species, but the invariable claim is already decided by class differences.
rationale: Which of these organs occur in fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals is standard anatomy in open species accounts and model-organism databases. Lungs are already coded as absent in most fishes, which is enough to test the only-these-two wording. A team can score the five organs by class from existing references without new dissection.

operationalization: Score a urinary bladder in birds, fishes, scaly reptiles and turtles. A bladder in a lizard, snake, bird or fish refutes the only-tortoises wording; absence in turtles refutes the exception.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: urinary bladder presence in birds, turtles, lizards, snakes and crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic coverage of the scaly reptiles and turtles in the scope

obstacles: Bladder presence is in prose accounts, not a character column, and is unstated for many species.
Some fishes have urinary bladders that are easy to overlook in general fish databases.
rationale: Urinary bladders of turtles and of many lizards are described in open herpetological accounts, which is enough to test the only-exception wording at group level. The character is not tabulated for every species, and fish bladders are inconsistently recorded. The group-level contrast can be compiled; a species-level universal cannot be downloaded.

operationalization: Score kidneys in birds, fishes, scaly reptiles and turtles. Kidneys in any bird, fish or non-chelonian reptile refute the absence claim; absence in turtles refutes the stated exception. Flattened avian kidneys still count as kidneys if they produce urine.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: kidney presence in birds, reptiles and fishes

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: the kidney of a teleost as a direct counterexample to absence in scaly or fish-like blooded animals

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: keeps kidney distinct from a vaguely kidney-like body

obstacles: Aristotle allows flattened kidney-like bodies in some birds, so a coder must decide whether those count as the organ he says is lacking.
rationale: Kidneys are class-level organs of fishes, birds and reptiles, and that fact is recorded in open anatomical accounts and in a model-fish database. The tortoises-only exception is therefore decidable without new dissection. The only real ambiguity is whether a lobulated avian kidney is the organ named in the claim, and that can be fixed from the same descriptions.

operationalization: In animals with paired kidneys, compare the craniocaudal position of the right and left organs. A species in which the left kidney sits higher refutes the universal. Humans are one species inside the scope, not the whole of it.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: right and left kidney position in one male and one female human

obstacles: Comparative positions are in veterinary anatomy papers, not a multi-species file.
Two human bodies cannot represent all animals that have kidneys.
rationale: Which kidney sits higher is a direct measurement, and it is known for humans and for a scatter of domestic mammals. Only the human pair is in a public image dataset, and even there the sample is two individuals. The universal over all kidney-bearing animals needs a compilation that does not yet exist as a dataset.

operationalization: Define laughter as a play vocalization elicited by tickling, then search for that response in humans and other mammals, especially apes and rodents. A tickle-evoked play call outside humans refutes uniqueness. A looser definition that requires propositional humor makes the claim nearly untestable.
obstacles: Laughter is not a field in trait databases, and ape and rat play vocalizations are in experimental papers.
Whether those calls are laughter is the operational dispute that decides the unique-to-humans claim.
rationale: Tickle-evoked play sounds in apes and rats are published observations, so a behavioral reading can be confronted without new experiments. There is no comparative dataset of the response, and a stricter reading on which only human laughter counts makes every non-human case irrelevant by definition. The assessment stays partial because the word laughter does not fix the criterion.

operationalization: For viviparous mammals with upper and lower incisors, count stomach chambers. More than one chamber in any such species refutes the single-stomach universal. The named genera are the minimum set; the universal requires the other incisor-bearing orders as well.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: stomach form and incisor presence for carnivores, perissodactyls, pigs, primates and rodents

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: diet and taxonomy of the mammals in scope; it does not itself count stomach chambers

obstacles: Stomach chamber number is prose in species accounts, although it is stable at the level of mammalian orders.
Incisors in both jaws excludes ruminants and must not be confused with camels, which lack upper incisors.
rationale: Monogastric versus multi-chamber stomachs, and the presence of upper incisors, are described for every mammalian order in open accounts. The pattern is uniform enough within orders that a team can score the incisor-bearing groups from those accounts. Chamber number is not a life-history column, but it does not need to be, because the ordinal anatomy is already published and consistent.

operationalization: Score horn presence, upper incisors and stomach-chamber number for bovids, deer, camels and chevrotains. Several stomachs in a hornless species, or a single stomach in a horned one, refutes the stated link. The chewing explanation is supported only if the extra chambers occur exactly where foregut fermentation compensates for dentition.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: rumen structure, horns and upper incisors in deer, bovids, camels and chevrotains

candidate_datasets.name: Mammal Diversity Database
candidate_datasets.role: lists the living ruminant and camelid families so hornless multi-stomach species are not omitted

obstacles: Camels and musk deer are hornless and multi-chambered, so they test the because-horned clause rather than the anatomy of sheep and cattle.
Chamber counts vary among foregut fermenters and need a threshold for several.
rationale: Stomach complexity, horns and upper teeth are all described for the relevant families in open mammal accounts, and the family list is closed. Hornless ruminants and camelids are in that list, so they discriminate a horn-based explanation from a dentition or fermentation explanation. The named livestock can be scored directly, and the rivals that lack horns can be scored from the same sources.

operationalization: Define rumination as regurgitation and rechewing of foregut contents, then search feeding observations for Sparisoma cretense and for other fishes. Oral scraping or pharyngeal milling without regurgitation does not count. Another ruminating fish, or no regurgitation in the parrotfish, refutes the corresponding part.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet and feeding notes for the Mediterranean parrotfish and other fishes

obstacles: Aristotle says apparently ruminates, and pharyngeal chewing is easily mistaken for cud-chewing.
The ancient Scarus may not be only Sparisoma cretense, and quantitative feeding observations are few.
rationale: Fish diet databases record that parrotfishes scrape and mill food, which is a proxy, not regurgitation. True rumination is rarely observed in fishes and is not a coded behavior. The single-exception claim can be probed with existing feeding notes and cannot be settled by them, because the notes do not use Aristotle's criterion.
